subtype: Approach: writing it down as soon as it is told [Action]
passage: Damini, look at this small diary I still keep. I'm Pankaj, and when I was ten, my teacher, Mr Kulkarni, called out what we needed for the next day's science class: a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper. Most children nodded and hoped to remember. I took out my little diary and wrote the four items at once, in a hurry, before the next lesson began. That night I checked it twice, once at dinner and once before sleep. In class, I was the only one with all four things. Writing had made my head free to think about the experiment.

qa.q: What four items did the teacher ask for?
qa.a: The teacher asked for a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper.

qa.q: Why did the narrator write the items at once?
qa.a: Pankaj wanted the list safe in the diary instead of in a head that might forget, and felt sure this would help.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped the narrator have all four items, and why?
qa.a: Writing them down at once and checking twice helped, because the list stayed correct and the narrator could check it later.

qa.q: How did the other children in the class fare?
qa.a: Most children only nodded and hoped to remember, and Pankaj was the only one with all four things, so the others probably missed some items.

grounding: Pankaj writes down the items the teacher names in a small diary at once, which frees the mind from holding them and lets the list be checked later.
